newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Pearson boosted by figures and fighting talk.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Pearson boosted by figures and fighting talk.

text.p: Pearson Plc Chief Executive Marjorie Scardino set a target of double digit annual earnings growth as the British media and leisure company beat expectations with its first half results.

Pearson, owner of prized assets such as the Financial Times newspaper and Penguin books, said profit from continuing operations almost doubled to 65.5 million pounds ($106.8 million) in the first six months of 1997. Earnings per share rose 50 percent to 6.0p while the interim dividend was increased nine percent to 6.9p.
Pearson shares, which have performed poorly in recent weeks, added 26.5p to 692.5p, up some four percent.
Scardino, a Texan who in January became the first woman to head a top British company, said she was pleased with the fruits of her first few months in the job.
"We feel really good about these half year results," she told a news conference.

She said that Pearson now aimed to deliver consistent earnings growth and set a second goal of doubling the company's value in the next five years. Its current market capitalisation is around four billion pounds.
"We would hope that if we produce this kind of performance our shares will get a re-rating," Scardino said.

Analysts said the goal of doubling the size of the company was rather meaningless since it was impossible to tell how the market as a whole would perform. But they welcomed her commitment to earnings growth and there were some early signs of a reappraisal of the stock.
Broker SBC Warburg raised its recommendation on the stock to "hold" from "reduce" while Henderson Crosthwaite raised its current year forecast to 290 million pounds from 280 million.
Most analysts are grouping their forecasts either side of the 300 million pound level, against 251 million last year.

Scardino said Pearson was reviewing a portfolio of stellar assets which include a television production arm, the Madame Tussaud's waxwork exhibition and a 50 percent stake in merchant bank Lazard Brothers.
"There may be a different cast of business characters but the goal will stay the same," she said.
Pearson said it was considering offers for medical publisher Churchill Livingstone, which produces physicians' bible Gray's Anatomy. It is likely to have a price tag of around $100 million.
Another likely disposal candidate is Pearson's remaining four percent indirect stake in pay television operator BSkyB Plc, worth some 340 million pounds at current values.
But Scardino virtually ruled out the sale of Pearson's TV arm, saying that it was one of the companies fastest growing businesses.

Finance Director John Makinson explained that the profit figure was flattered by one-off costs taken last year. But he added that underlying profits had increased by 5.8 million pounds despite the impact of the strong pound and losses from Britain's new Channel 5 TV network.
The company reported a surge in first half profits at the Financial Times and a strong performance from Penguin as last December's acquisition of U.S. publisher Putnam Berkley was integrated swiftly.

"We expect further growth in group revenues and operating profits in the second half of the year, tempered by revenue investment in the Financial Times newspaper, Financial Times Information and Channel 5, as well as by the impact of sterling's strength," Scardino said.

Financial Times Information provides electronic financial information while Pearson has a large stake in Channel 5, the national commercial TV station launched in Britain in March. Pearson had start-up losses of 11.7 million pounds from Channel 5 in the first half.
Makinson said the strength of sterling, if maintained, would wipe some 20 million pounds off the pre-tax figure for the full year and cut sales revenues by 120 million. ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
